doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: After the war: big-band era and postwar medical planning
summary: Budd digresses on baby-boom predictions, hospital building and the growth of medical schools.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: ...who’s really into it. When you came back to this country, it was still the big band era.
Yes, I think that started about 1950 probably, I’m not sure. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-
Yeah, after the way, ‘46, 7... And then jazz changed a lot.

Yes, about that time. It’s when that new generation of new guys — I was interested in that. One of the things I learned in medicine, this has nothing to do with this so you may want to cut this out, but I was interested in medical politics and economics and I was on a committee from the Academy of Medicine from the labor union and from the hospitals and from the insurance industry in Cleveland. At that time they were planning about things after the war, and they established the fact that the commonest age for any woman in those age to have a baby was age 24. The war ended in 1945 and so there were a tremendous amount of young men coming back from war that would be getting married, they were positive in those later years, and so in 1946 these marriages would take place, and 24 years from 1946 was 1970. So they said 1970 — isn’t it 46, 56, yes, 24 years from ‘46 that it would be the biggest birth rate you’ve seen in years in the United States, and there’s going to be more hospitals necessary and more doctors necessary and so they said they had enormous programs. In fact Senator Burton from Cleveland, the Hill Burton Act, Senator Hill from Alabama, but the Hill Burton Act was enacted. Every town and community should have a hospital, they’ll need all these hospitals. And so there was a tremendous increase in hospital building about that time, from 1970 on. And in the late 70’s they wanted more medical schools they needed more doctors. And so at that time in 1974 or 5, there were 80 medical schools in the United States. And in the next 20 years they had 40 more medical schools. There’s now 126. And of course now they’ve got more than they need. They have so many that are in very elite specialties. A lot of guys go into that. Another thing they did was import people from other countries, deprived countries, they needed doctors there. So they allowed people to come here and stay and get training, but they want to go home to do good for their own country. And many of them did come, but when they got here they didn’t want to go home. The only way they could stay here was to marry an American girl, and a lot of them did. And of course most of them with their skills and their interest, a high percentage of them become plastic surgeons and cardiac surgeons, thoracic surgeons, not many went into the only work of general practice. Although now general practice is becoming very popular and taking its right place, although they call it family practice now. But it doesn’t include obstetrics and stuff like that. But those are changes in medicine which are different and are not pertinent in this interview I don’t think.
